# A28-S143: Preparatory research

*Research text; source extract.*

[████]

Yes. Ars Electronica is central to Linz's post-industrial self-reinvention.
It began in 1979, in a city marked by heavy industry and the aftershocks of
the 1973 oil crisis; from the outset, it framed itself not as a celebration
of technology alone, but as a forum on art, technology, and society. The
first festival opened on 18 September 1979, with the robot SPA-12
delivering a greeting and the Linzer Klangwolke helping turn the city
itself into a public stage. Over time, the festival was joined by the Prix
Ars Electronica in 1987, the Ars Electronica Center and Futurelab in 1996,
and the expanded Center in 2009. Ars Electronica Linz GmbH & Co KG remains
structurally tied to municipal governance: it is formally a company of the
City of Linz.

If one asks which projects had the "most impact," there is no official Ars
Electronica ranking based on political consequences. The cleanest proxy is
a combination of first prizes, recurrent institutional visibility, and
durable relevance in public debates on surveillance, borders, democracy,
infrastructure, and automation. On that basis, Ars Electronica's political
history can be read in four strands: first, media art about state power,
surveillance, and borders; second, projects on digital communities and
democratic action; third, robotics and AI as political form; and fourth,
Linz-specific urban and civic infrastructure projects.

In institutional terms, Ars Electronica matters politically because it was
never just a festival. It became a municipal-cultural apparatus for staging
debate in public space. That is visible in the way Linz was used not merely
as host city but as medium: the Klangwolke, the Danube frontage, the
Hauptplatz, later the Ars Electronica Center, and then POSTCITY all
functioned as civic infrastructures for public discourse. This is why the
history of Ars Electronica in Linz is not separable from local cultural
policy. It is, in effect, a long experiment in urban cultural governance
through media art.

The strongest first-prize projects with explicitly political angles include
Paolo Cirio's *Loophole for All*, awarded the 2014 Golden Nica in
Interactive Art. Ars Electronica itself described it as a major work of
social criticism; the project exposed offshore tax structures by making
corporate shell identities symbolically available to everyone, thereby
converting tax avoidance into a visible political-aesthetic problem. It is
one of the clearest cases where Ars Electronica elevated media art into a
critique of global finance and legal asymmetry.

Another key project is Christoph Wachter and Mathias Jud's *Can you hear
me?*, which received the 2016 Golden Nica in Interactive Art+. The project
responded directly to the surveillance regime revealed by Edward Snowden.
It worked in Berlin's federal government district and addressed the problem
of monitored communication by proposing autonomous communication
infrastructures. In Ars Electronica's framing, it was a direct intervention
into contemporary conditions of espionage, surveillance, and state power.

In the field of democracy and networked protest, *Be Water by Hong Kongers*,
awarded the 2020 Golden Nica in Digital Communities, is one of the most
unambiguous political winners in the history of the Prix. Ars Electronica
presented it as dedicated to the Hong Kong protest movement and as a case
study in digital activism under pressure. Here the awarded object was not a
discrete art object in the older sense, but a distributed political-media
formation. That marks an important shift in the Prix itself: from rewarding
representation to rewarding collective tactics and civic communication.

A further milestone is *Avatar Robot Cafe DAWN ver.β*, the 2022 Golden Nica
in Digital Communities. This is less overtly partisan, but politically
substantial. The project uses teleoperated robot avatars to enable people
with severe disabilities or chronic illness to participate in work and
public life. Its political force lies in labor, accessibility, and civic
inclusion: robotics here is not spectacle but an institutional design
question about who gets to appear and act in social space.

For the nexus of robotics and politics more strictly understood, Ars
Electronica offers several strong cases. The inaugural symbol is SPA-12 in
1979: a robot delivering a public address at the birth of the festival.
This was not yet "robot politics" in the contemporary AI-governance sense,
but it established a durable trope: the machine as public speaker and
political sign. Decades later, Kathrin Stumreich's *Sovereignty* sharpened
that trope. In this work, a flag is moved by a robot arm and intersected by
laser-triggered sound; Ars Electronica explicitly interprets it as a
meditation on control, algorithmic determination, surveillance, and
self-determination. The work is not a Golden Nica winner, but it is an
important institutional reference point for thinking robotics through
political symbolism.

The 2025 Golden Nica in Artificial Life & Intelligence, Paula Gaetano Adi's
*Guanaquerx*, extends this into decolonial robotics. Ars Electronica
describes it as the first robot to cross the Andes, and emphasizes that it
is not merely an engineering feat but a poetic and political operation.
That matters because it shifts the discourse from robots as instruments of
efficiency to robots as agents in histories of territory, extraction, and
colonial knowledge.

A related non-first-prize example is *Requiem for an Exit*, highlighted in
the Prix archive in 2024. Ars Electronica's description is unusually
direct: the robotic installations by Frode Oldereid and Thomas Kvam
explored the intersections of technology, ideology, and collective memory,
evoking the aesthetics of political mass movements and the broken language
of totalitarianisms. This is a strong case for your "robots and politics"
line of inquiry, even if it is better read as a curatorial and archival
node than as one of the canonical all-time winners.

If one broadens from the Prix to the wider Ars ecosystem, the 2025 STARTS
Prize project *AI War Cloud Database* is especially important. Ars
Electronica presents it as a mapping of automated warfare systems and their
overlap with everyday consumer technologies. The project is political in a
very literal sense: it links AI, logistics, military decision-making, and
civilian platforms, and asks who builds the technological stack of
contemporary power. It is less about Linz specifically than about Ars
Electronica's present role as a platform for infrastructural critique.

Now to the Linz-specific layer. Here the key point is that some of the most
politically relevant Ars projects are not prize winners at all, but urban
interfaces commissioned with or for the city. The first and most
consequential example is the Linzer Klangwolke, launched with the first
festival in 1979. It made the city a distributed acoustic-public medium and
remains one of the emblematic cases of "art in public space" in Linz. Its
significance is civic rather than merely aesthetic: it re-scripted how
residents encountered culture collectively.

A second local-infrastructural line runs through municipal digital
services. *Hotspot Linz*, presented in the 2005 Ars context, was an
initiative of the City of Linz in cooperation with Ars Electronica and
Liwest, with a web portal realized by the Ars Electronica Futurelab. The
project accompanied the city's rollout of several hundred public hotspots
and even included a virtual guestbook for public exchange via internet,
SMS, and MMS. This is a good example of Ars Electronica acting as mediator
between municipal infrastructure, communication technology, and
participatory urban branding.

A third case is the *neighborhood* / *We Are Linz* constellation shown in
2013. According to the archive, it was a project of the Unternehmensgruppe
Stadt Linz, the city's municipal services provider, developed by Ars
Electronica. Its interactive installations presented information about the
city, local history, culture, and infrastructure. This is not radical
politics, but it is politically relevant because it turns municipal service
provision into an interactive cultural interface. In other words, Ars
Electronica here functions as a designer of civic legibility.

A fourth case is the POSTCITY phase. From 2015 onward, Ars Electronica used
the former postal logistics complex as its central festival site. This was
more than a venue change. Ars texts repeatedly tied POSTCITY to questions
of future mobility, urban planning, social organization, and security; the
2015 festival theme "POST CITY. Habitats for the 21st Century" explicitly
centered the city as a political problem-space. The archive also notes that
concerns over protocols, standards, and mobility in the 21st-century city
were part of the conceptual frame around this move. In that sense, POSTCITY
was a temporary urban laboratory built inside a redundant logistics
infrastructure.

This local dimension matters because Ars Electronica's politics in Linz is
often infrastructural rather than ideological. The institution repeatedly
translates municipal systems into public interfaces: telecommunications,
transport, urban redevelopment, cultural venues, civic identity, tourism,
and digital participation. Even small details, such as partnerships with
LINZ AG around public transport access to festival sites, show how Ars
operates within the grain of city governance rather than outside it.

So, if I reduce the whole history to a workable analytic map, I would say
this. Ars Electronica's most important political contribution is not one
single prizewinner. It is the long-term coupling of media art to public
infrastructure in a mid-sized European city. The most influential
first-prize works in explicitly political terms are probably *Loophole for
All* for tax justice, *Can you hear me?* for surveillance and autonomous
communication, *Be Water by Hong Kongers* for protest and digital
democracy, and *Avatar Robot Cafe DAWN ver.β* for disability, labor, and
inclusion. For robotics and politics specifically, the strongest line runs
from SPA-12 in 1979 to *Sovereignty*, *Requiem for an Exit*, and
*Guanaquerx*. For Linz-local politics, the crucial projects are the
Klangwolke, the Ars Electronica Center as civic anchor, *Hotspot Linz*, *We
Are Linz*, and the POSTCITY turn.

For your purposes, a useful distinction would be between three levels of
politics. First, representational politics: artworks about surveillance,
borders, finance, protest. Second, operational politics: projects that
prototype alternative communication, accessibility, or collective
organization. Third, urban-institutional politics: Ars Electronica as a
municipal platform that reorganizes how Linz sees itself and how local
infrastructures become publicly intelligible. In Linz, the third level is
the most specific one. It is what makes Ars Electronica different from a
biennial that merely visits a city.

I can turn this into a more formal research memo next: with chronology,
shortlist of 15 projects, category labels, and a distinction between Prix
winners, festival commissions, and Linz-specific infrastructure projects.
Linz Geschichte der Gewerkschaften …

Yes. For Linz, the history of trade unions is at its core a history
 of industrialization, the workers' movement, Austrofascism,
 reconstruction after 1945, and the large industrial enterprises around the
 voest. The city is the central place for this in Upper Austria. The
 Austrian trade union movement emerged since the 1870s,
 was 1934 banned and 1945 newly founded in the ÖGB. In Linz,
 this general development was particularly condensed because industry,
 municipal politics, and workers' organizations converged closely here.

For Upper Austria it is also important that the institutional representation
of employees was anchored early in Linz. The Chamber of Labor
Upper Austria held its constitutive meeting on 21 May 1921 in the Linz
Town Hall. The AK explicitly describes this founding as the result of
decades of trade union work. This shows: Linz was not only
an industrial location, but also an administrative and organizational center of
organized workers' interests.

Historically, five phases can be distinguished for Linz. First, the
Formation phase in the late 19 century: with industrialization,
Club activities, educational associations and early trade union
The form of organization. Secondly, the strong expansion in the First Republic,
as workers' organizations also municipally and culturally in Linz
became visible. Thirdly the break from 1934 to 1945: In Austrofascism
free trade unions were smashed; under National Socialism changed
Linz as an industrial and "leader city" massively. Fourthly the
Reconstruction from 1945 with the re-establishment of the ÖGB and the expansion of the
Social partnership. Fifth, the post-war era of big industry, in
who the voest and its works council culture the union profile of
Especially influenced Linz.

For Linz in the narrow sense, the voest is the central node. After the war
the Linz plants were 1945 reorganized under public administration
and renamed VÖEST. This not only created an industrial
core company but also a social and political space where
works council, co-determination and trade union representation of interests over
decades were extraordinarily important. When talking about trade union history
in Linz, one almost always also speaks about the history of
the steel industry, nationalized industry and company
co-determination.

Another Linz place of memory is the Jägermayrhof. The AK
Upper Austria has used it since the late 1950s as an educational center;
at the same time it itself points to its political prehistory and its
role in the struggle against Austrofascism. This is relevant because
trade union history in Linz is not only factory history but
also history of education, associations and memory.

Institutionally, Linz remains the center of trade union organization
in Upper Austria to this day. The state organization of the ÖGB Upper Austria is located in
Volksgartenstraße 34 in Linz; the AK Upper Austria also has its headquarters there in
immediate proximity. This is not merely an address but an expression of a
long historical concentration of employee representation in the
city.

If you want to read this politically, then Linz is a particularly
instructive case: Trade unions here were never just wage politics. They were
part of urban development, social infrastructure, political
education and the cultural self-description of an industrial city. Exactly
for this reason, Linz is also interesting for questions of local democracy, municipal politics
and public culture.

For your Ars Electronica question, the connection would then be this: Ars
Electronica rather stands for the postindustrial, media-cultural
reinvention of Linz; trade union history stands for the
industrial and social-democratic foundation of the city. The exciting thing is
precisely the transition from the steel city to the city of culture and technology.

I can develop that next for you in three possible forms: as a
concise timeline, as a systematic overview "Linz as a
trade union city", or as a connecting thread between
workers' movement, voest, city politics and Ars Electronica.
History Linz Uni JKU / Art Uni / Bruckner / Art Uni ~ Education
infrastructure…

Yes. A clear development line can be described for Linz: from the
industrial and administrative city to the university and educational city. The
actual expansion of the tertiary educational infrastructure began in the
post-war period. City and state operated for decades the establishment
of a university; 1966the later JKU was opened. In the 1970s
further university foundations followed, including the art university and
the current Catholic private university. In the
city historiography, this is explicitly marked as a milestone of
urban development.

The JKU is the turning point. Legally, the University of
Social and Economic Sciences in Linz was established 1962; it was ceremonially opened
on 8 October 1966. Since 1975 it has borne the name Johannes Kepler
University Linz. Its later expansion to include law as well as
technical and natural sciences made it the actual engine
of the scientific infrastructure of the city. The JKU itself today describes
itself as a comparatively young university with around 25.000
students and just under 4.000 staff; at the same time, it points to
its early pioneering role, for example in establishing computer science as a field of study
in Austria.

Spatially and in terms of city history, the JKU is not only a university,
but an infrastructure project in the north of Linz. The campus in
Dornach/Auhof was part of a long-term expansion of the city and
knowledge landscape. The university complex created a new educational space
beyond the historic city center. At the same time, the area is not historically
innocent: The JKU-published history of the site refers
to NS forced labor and camp contexts in the vicinity of the later campus.
Thus, the educational infrastructure of Linz is also embedded in memory-political
layers.

The Art University Linz follows a different logic. It is not a
campus university on the city outskirts but an inner-city cultural and
educational institution. Its history begins 1947 with the "Art School
of the City of Linz." It occupied spaces in the western bridgehead building on the
main square 8; later more locations were added. From this art school
the University of Artistic and Industrial
Design and finally today's Art University Linz evolved. Its
history is therefore closely linked to municipal cultural policy and to the
claim to inscribe design, art, architecture and media-based
practice in the urban center.

Especially at the Art University, the architectural and political history
of the site is central. The bridgehead buildings on the main square were planned and built during the
Nazi era; residents were displaced and
expropriated for this, and forced labor played a role in the construction. The university
actively addresses this building history today. This is important for Linz,
because here educational infrastructure, cityscape and Nazi past directly
intersect. The Art University is therefore not only a place of education,
but also a place of institutionalized historical reflection in the
urban space.

Content-wise, the Art University represents the shift that has characterized Linz since the late
20 century: away from a pure industrial city, toward
a city that understands art, design, media, architecture and critical
theory as part of its identity. Its official profile speaks
of a "critical experimental zone" and emphasizes its focuses
in art, design, space, media and research. In the context of Linz's
urban development, it is therefore less a mass university and more a
signal institution: it anchors cultural and aesthetic forms of knowledge
right in the city.

The Anton Bruckner Private University forms the third major pole of
Linz's educational infrastructure. It is the artistic university for
music, acting and dance. Its current institution, according to its own
account, can look back on more than 200 years of history as an artistic
training institution; since 2004 it has been accredited as a private university of
the state of Upper Austria. The decisive turning point was thus
the transformation of the former Bruckner Conservatory into a university.
This elevated musical and performative education in Linz
institutionally to a new level.

The Bruckner University is also strongly legible through its location. Its
current building in the Pöstlingberg/Hagenberg area links art university,
landscape and outskirts location. The state of Upper Austria emphasizes the function
of the university as one of the few specialized universities for music
and performing arts in Austria. This complements the Linz
university system with those fields that neither JKU nor the Art University
cover in this form: highly specialized artistic practice, pedagogical
training and performative research. Its 12institutes and the
doctoral school also mark the expansion toward a full university
structure.

Systematically, one can distinguish the three institutions as follows. The JKU
stands for scientific-technical and social-scientific
scaling. The Art University stands for urban cultural concentration
and critical design practice. The Bruckner University stands for the
musical-performative axis of the city. Together they create an
unusually dense configuration for a city the size of Linz:
campus university, inner-city art university and specialized
music and performing university. This triad explains part of the
structural change of Linz very precisely.

If you sum it up as “educational infrastructure,” it's not just about
 buildings and study places. It's about a city knowledge order. The
 JKU forms the large research and training apparatus; the
 art university links education to the symbolic core of the city; the
 Bruckner University strengthens music and performance culture. In combination
 with other institutions like Wissensturm, city library, and cultural
 infrastructures, a structure emerged that gradually1945 redefined Linz after 
. The city's cultural development plan explicitly emphasizes the importance of
 tertiary and cultural education for urban development
.

Historically, I would distinguish three phases. First, the
post-war reconstruction and the institutional founding of new universities from the
1960s onward. Second, the differentiation since the 1970s to 2000s
when art and music university structures were expanded or newly established.
Third, the phase in which Linz uses these educational institutions as
part of its international positioning: not only industry,
but science, art, technology and performance. In this
perspective, JKU, Art University and Bruckner University are part of
the hard urban infrastructure of Linz, not just its cultural
appendage.

If you want, in the next step I can make a concise timeline
1945–2026 or an analytical matrix with columns founding, location,
 sponsorship, profile, city-political function, and symbolic role in
 Linz.
